prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated without light-shift perturbation, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B032 to B007 with Katori and Ye. The reason is not the support count, which I do not treat as evidence, but that the chair's question to me exposes a defect I cannot repair. A prize for B032 would have to name three people among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert, and the scientific record, as I recall it, does not let the committee say who identified what first: the Evans-Cohen-Morriss steady-state relation, the Evans-Searles transient theorem, Jarzynski's equality and Crooks' detailed relation are different statements with different proofs, and Seifert's contribution is the trajectory-level framework rather than one of the theorems. I could not state a citation that is fair to all of them, and I do not believe external expert reports would shrink the list to three, because the difficulty is that several distinct exact results all deserve credit, not that facts are missing. Against that, B007 has the clean attribution I asked for in B032: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is the identifiable enabling idea, and Ye's group took the system to record accuracy and stability and showed that interactions between the many interrogated atoms are physics in their own right. Independent laboratories reproduce 1e-18 performance, so the result is understood and tested, which is what I care about. My earlier worry that this was an engineering of a light shift is weaker after reading the exchange: the point is that choosing the wavelength where both clock states shift equally converts a many-body ensemble into a statistical resource, and that is a mechanism, simply and generally stated. I rank it first on scientific grounds now and not as a compromise.
statement.case_against: Novelty remains the real objection. The 2005 prize (comb) and the 2012 prize (ion control) cover neighbouring ground, and the best ion clocks reach comparable accuracy, so the citation has to say that the new element is the magic-wavelength lattice and the use of many neutral atoms, not precision clocks as such. Priority outside the credited pair (Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov, the ion-clock groups) is unsettled, and I am relying on recollection of the 2001-2003 record, which I cannot check. The SI second has not yet been redefined; I do not think that is a reason to wait, because the demonstrated and independently compared performance is the scientific content, but I accept that others may weigh it differently. Finally, B032 deserves a second look in a later year if the field converges on a short list of originators, and I do not want my change here to be read as a judgment that it lacks merit.

responses.point: Pearce argues that going from the 1e-15 regime to 1e-18 with a new trapping scheme is a qualitative change, not a refinement, and that nobody has produced an objection to B007 that survives scrutiny.
responses.response: You persuade me on the second point more than the first. The factor of a thousand matters, but what persuades me is the mechanism: the magic wavelength removes the perturbation by the trap itself, so the ensemble gain is not paid for in systematics. That is a simple and general idea, and it answers my round-1 worry that the prize would reward engineering. I still think the citation must state this mechanism explicitly, otherwise the 2005 and 2012 overlap is not addressed. On your invitation to supply a clean three-name story for B032, I cannot, and I withdraw it as my first choice for that reason.

responses.point: Lindroth answers my significance question by saying that the lattice clock redefines what can be measured and has already produced a laboratory test of the gravitational redshift at millimetre scale, and that the two credited names track the two decisive steps.
responses.response: I accept that answer. A laboratory measurement of the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-sized sample is a statement about nature that comes out of the instrument, and it makes B007 more than a metrology prize. I would ask you and Kroll, as the atomic physicists, to confirm against the record that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice spectroscopy precede or are contemporaneous with Ye's, and that Lemonde's and Derevianko's contributions are of a different kind (accurate theory of the shift, early realisations) rather than a competing claim to the central idea. If that check holds, two names is defensible, and I would add that I regard credit for Ye as resting on accuracy, stability and the many-body clock work, not on being first.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B012 first because IceCube is a discovery in the sense that nature supplied an unanticipated clue, and asks whether the committee should favour a stronger discovery case with narrower support.
responses.response: I share the instinct that a prize should reward something learned about nature, and I raised a similar worry about B007 in round 1. But I do not think B012 resolves it for me: the diffuse flux is established, yet the source picture is at about four sigma for NGC 1068 and the origin of most of the flux is open, so what has been learned is that the signal exists, not what produces it. The attribution you concede, a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, is the same kind of problem that moved me off B032. If the committee considers a second part, I would hold B012 for a later year, when source identification is firmer, rather than force it now into a two-name credit.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps a pull toward condensed-matter candidates B018 and B005, noting the open pairing mechanism and sample dependence in B005 and the absence of Metzner from the B018 credit.
responses.response: I agree with the objection to B018 as credited, since the infinite-dimension limit starts with Metzner and Vollhardt and a three-name set that omits him describes the discovery unfairly. For B005 I would add that the flat-band mechanism is understood well enough, but the pairing question and sample dependence mean the physics is still being written. I would not support either as a second part this year, and the three-person limit leaves one extra name beside Katori and Ye, which none of the condensed-matter candidates can use cleanly.

uncertainties: Whether the 2001-2003 priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice spectroscopy supports Katori and Ye as the two names, and how Lemonde, Derevianko and Pal'chikov should be weighed; I am working from recollection and ask that Lindroth, Kroll or Olsson check it.
Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct enabling idea or as an evolutionary step after the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I now lean to the former but see the other reading as legitimate.
Whether a second part is worth pursuing at all given the three-person limit; I see no candidate with a settled interpretation and a credit of one or two names, and B032 is not one.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal needed. I know none of Katori, Ye, Jarzynski, Evans, Seifert or the other shortlisted names as collaborators; my frequent co-authors are in turbulence and population genetics. Gothenburg colleagues on the committee (Johansson, Olsson) are in the same physics environment, with no specific collaboration relevant to B007. Unchanged from round 1.
